facts.statement: It is debated whether Palaelodus were divers or swam using stiff toes to feed on larvae and snails.
facts.quote: Their precise lifestyle is disputed, with researchers in the past suggesting they may have been divers

facts.statement: Palaelodus was most abundant during the Late Oligocene to Middle Miocene periods.

facts.statement: Isolated remains suggest that Palaelodus or a relative survived until the Pleistocene in Australia.

facts.statement: Alphonse Milne-Edwards described the genus Palaelodus in 1863 based on fossils from the Saint-Gérand-le-Puy area in France.
facts.quote: The genus Palaelodus was first described by French scientist Alphonse Milne-Edwards in 1863 on the basis of fossils discovered in France's early Miocene deposits of the Saint-Gérand-le-Puy area

facts.statement: Palaelodus remains were first recognized in Australia in 1982 but were not formally described until 1998.
facts.quote: Palaelodus remains were first recognized in Australia in 1982, but not described until 1998

facts.statement: Largely complete crania of Palaelodus were not described until 1992 by Cheneval and Escuillié.
facts.quote: unambiguous fossils of the skull were long unknown until largely complete crania were described by Cheneval and Escuillié in 1992

facts.statement: Palaelodus kurochkini was described from Miocene remains found in Mongolia.
facts.quote: Palaelodus kurochkini was described from remains dating to the Miocene of Mongolia

facts.statement: The most recently named species, P. haroldocontii, comes from the Late Miocene of Argentina.
facts.quote: The most recently named species is P. haroldocontii from the Late Miocene of Argentina

facts.statement: The name Palaelodus comes from Ancient Greek words meaning "ancient" and "inhabitant of marshes".
facts.quote: The name Palaelodus derives from the Ancient Greek "palaios" for "ancient" and "elodes" which means "inhabitant of marshes"

facts.statement: Palaelodus ambiguus is one of the best-known species of the genus.
facts.quote: P. ambiguus is one of the best known species of Palaelodus

facts.statement: Palaelodus haroldocontii is considered a large species, larger than P. pledgei, P. gracilipes, and P. crassipes.
facts.quote: P. haroldocontii is regarded as a large species in the range of most of the other Palaelodus species sans P. pledgei, P. gracilipes and P. crassipes

facts.statement: Palaelodus aotearoa was a medium-sized bird substantially larger than the contemporary Australian species P. pledgei.
facts.quote: P. aotearoa was a medium sized palaelodid and substantially larger than the contemporary P. pledgei

facts.statement: Some traits suggest Palaelodus kurochkini may represent a distinct genus rather than belonging to Palaelodus or Megapaloelodus.
facts.quote: Due to some traits differentiating it from both Palaelodus and Megapaloelodus, it may actually represent a distinct genus

facts.statement: Recent research casts doubt on whether Pleistocene remains found in Australia belong to Palaelodus wilsoni.
facts.quote: more recent research has left it doubtful whether or not the Pleistocene remains belong to P. wilsoni

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether Palaelodus gracilipes is a distinct species or just smaller individuals of the type species, noting that synonymizing them without further study might be premature.
facts.quote: According to Mlíkovský, this species only represents smaller individuals of the type species, but other researchers argue that declaring the two species synonyms, while not out of the question, would be premature without an extensive look into the available material.

facts.statement: There is an ongoing scientific debate about whether Palaelodus crassipes is a separate species or simply larger individuals of the type species, with some experts urging more detailed examination of European fossils before merging them.
facts.quote: According to Mlíkovský, this species only represents larger individuals of the type species. Other researchers however argue that declaring the two species synonyms would be premature until the European material is examined in greater detail.

facts.statement: The species Megapaloelodus goliath was originally classified as a type of Palaelodus but was later reclassified into the genus Megapaloelodus because of its more robust physical structure.
facts.quote: Megapaloelodus goliath was originally described as a species of Palaelodus, but later moved to the American genus Megapaloelodus due to its more robust morphology separating it from the contemporary Palaelodus ambiguus.

facts.statement: The extinct crane Pliogrus germanicus is now considered a type of palaelodid and may belong to the genus Palaelodus.
facts.quote: The crane Pliogrus germanicus is now considered to be a type of palaelodid, possibly in the genus Palaelodus.

facts.statement: Palaelodus has a unique trait involving the position and development of nasal gland depressions located between its eye sockets, distinguishing its skull from all other known birds.
facts.quote: Among its autapomorphic traits is the position and development of the fossae glandulae nasales, two depressions for the nasal glands situated between the orbits of the animal.

facts.statement: The temporal fossae of Palaelodus show an intermediate condition between grebes and flamingos, being more pronounced than in flamingos but not as deep as in grebes.
facts.quote: The temporal fossae form somewhat of an intermediary between grebes and flamingos, more pronounced than in the later but not as deep as in the former.

facts.statement: The skull of Palaelodus clearly shows the presence of salt glands.
facts.quote: The skull of Palaelodus also clearly shows the presence of salt glands.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Mainz Basin and Saint-Gérand-le-Puy show that the notarium of Palaelodus consists of five fused vertebrae, unlike the four found in all living mirandornithes.
facts.quote: Specimens from the Mainz Basin as well as Saint-Gérand-le-Puy both show that the notarium, a series of fused vertebrae of the shoulder girdle, consists of five vertebrae rather than the four seen in all extant mirandornithes.

facts.statement: The middle toe bones of Palaelodus are compressed side-to-side, deep, and have weakly developed convex joints without a furrow, differing from those of flamingos.
facts.quote: The pedal phalanges, the bones that make up the middle toes, of Palaelodus are compressed mediolaterally unlike those of flamingos, deep and with weakly developed convex distal articulation points that lack a furrow.

facts.statement: The pelvis of Palaelodus is narrower than that of extant wading birds.
facts.quote: The pelvis also differs from flamingos, being more narrower than in the extant waders.

facts.statement: Palaelodus is considered an important evolutionary link between flamingos and their closest relatives, the diving grebes, within the clade Mirandornithes.
facts.quote: Palaeolodids such as Palaelodus are considered to be an important link in understanding the relationship between flamingos and their next closest relatives, the diving grebes with which they from the clade Mirandornithes.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest Palaelodus was a diver using webbed feet for propulsion, but this hypothesis has been questioned by others who propose alternative lifestyles.
facts.quote: Cheneval and Escuillié both suggest that Palaelodus may have been a diver using its webbed feet for propulsion, however this hypothesis has been questioned by the works of Mayr as well as Worthy and colleagues, both of whom suggest different alternatives.

facts.statement: There is a debate over Palaelodus' lifestyle: Worthy et al. (2010) suggest they were wading birds similar to flamingos, while Mayr suggests a swimming lifestyle.
facts.quote: In Worthy et al. (2010) it is suggested that palaelodids were wading birds, more akin to flamingos, while publications by Mayr suggest a swimming lifestyle.

facts.statement: Mayr argues that traits like compressed toes and reduced toe flexibility in Palaelodus support a swimming lifestyle, suggesting the webbed feet acted as stiff paddles.
facts.quote: Mayr meanwhile specifically points to several traits that according to him support a swimming lifestyle. The compression of the toes is unlike what is seen in any modern wading bird, while the decreased ability to flex the toes suggests the use of the webbed feet as stiff paddles.

facts.statement: Researchers proposed that Palaelodus may have had an enlarged tongue and shown early signs of filter feeding.
facts.quote: Cheneval and Escuillié proposed that the deep mandible of Palaelodus may have housed an enlarged tongue similar to that of flamingos and that these birds may have shown the first signs of becoming filter feeders.

facts.statement: Mayr argued that despite a possible enlarged tongue, Palaelodus lacked the bill structure needed to filter water like adult flamingos.
facts.quote: Although not directly disputing the presence of an enlarged tongue, Mayr points out that the bill of Palaelodus lacked the widened rim that holds the keratinous lamellae that allow flamingos to filter water.

facts.statement: Enlarged fossae on the mandible suggest Palaelodus used head movement for foraging in a way different from flamingos.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the enlarged fossae on the sides of the mandibular ramus indicate that movement of the head played a greater role in foraging than it does for flamingos, pointing to a more conventional method of feeding.

facts.statement: Palaelodus likely assumed a different feeding position than flamingos because its spine lacked a pronounced kink.
facts.quote: As this kink is not nearly as pronounced in Palaelodus, they likely assumed a different position while feeding.

facts.statement: Salt glands indicate Palaelodus foraged in saline or brackish waters.
facts.quote: The presence of salt glands indicates that regardless of the details of their diet, they must have foraged in saline or at least brackish waters like flamingos.

facts.statement: Milne-Edwards proposed that Palaelodus diet included larvae of caddisflies and snails found at Saint-Gérand-le-Puy.
facts.quote: Milne-Edwards proposed that this could contain the larvae of caddisflies and snails, which were particularly abundant at Saint-Gérand-le-Puy.

facts.statement: It is possible Palaelodids specialized in feeding on small invertebrates, setting the groundwork for later flamingo filter feeding.
facts.quote: It is therefore possible that Palaelodids and related genera were specialised in feeding on small invertebrates and subsequently set the groundwork for the more derived filter feeding apparatus of phoenicopterids.

facts.statement: Worthy and colleagues argue that thousands of bones in France suggest European Palaelodus lived in large flocks.
facts.quote: Worthy and colleagues argue that the discovery of thousands of bones in France could indicate that the European Palaelodus species may have lived in large flocks like modern flamingos.

facts.statement: Australian and New Zealand Palaelodus species may have been less social due to few bones found across multiple localities.
facts.quote: Species from Australia and New Zealand meanwhile may have been less social based on the fact that only few bones are known across multiple localities.

facts.statement: In Neogene Australia, Palaelodus species profited from salt lakes in the Lake Eyre Basin sharing habitat with derived flamingos like Phoenicopterus novaehollandiae.
facts.quote: In Neogene Australia Palaelodus species greatly profited from the availability of salt lakes in the Lake Eyre Basin, where the two recognized species shared their habitat with more derived species of flamingos such as Phoenicopterus novaehollandiae.

facts.statement: Juvenile specimens at Australian lake deposits show Palaelodus bred and nested in these localities.
facts.quote: The presence of juvenile specimens at the Australian lake deposits furthermore shows that these birds bred and nested in these localities.

facts.statement: P. aotearoa was found in the Bannockburn Formation sediments of the 5600 km2 paleo-Lake Manuherikia fed by a river delta in New Zealand.
facts.quote: In New Zealand P. aotearoa was found in what is now the Bannockburn Formation, the sediments of the 5600 km2 paleo-Lake Manuherikia which was fed by a river delta.

facts.statement: The environment preserving P. haroldocontii in Argentina is interpreted as a river system with floodplains, lagoons, and an ephemeral lake.
facts.quote: The environment that preserves the remains of P. haroldocontii in Argentina has been interpreted as a river system featuring floodplains and lagoons as well as an ephemeral lake, matching the types of biomes inhabited by other species of this genus.

facts.statement: The extinction of Palaelodus may be related to the disappearance of salt lakes, as seen in Australia after lake drying and possibly in Argentina after the "Age of Austral Plains" arid pulse.
facts.quote: The extinction of Palaelodus may be locally related to the disappearance of the aforementioned salt lakes, as evidenced by the fate of the Australian palaelodids and crown flamingos after the drying of Central Australia's lakes and possibly the extinction of Palaelodus in Argentina following an arid pulse known as the "Age of Austral Plains".
